items.title: From Legacy to Future-Proof: Implementing SAP MDG Cloud Ready Mode and Go-live
items.author: steffen_ulmer
items.text:
Hi SAP Community 
 I supported this project as SAP Trusted Advisor and Focus TQM: This is what we built, and what I took away from it: 
 In September 2026, a leading retail group went live with SAP MDG (Cloud-Ready Mode) . Not a pilot, not a proof of concept!: A full production go-live , replacing a legacy system that had reached its limits. 
 What made this project particularly interesting was the technology choice: the customer implemented SAP MDG in Cloud Ready Mode , the newest MDG innovation mode that bets fully on the latest SAP stack and Clean Core. The customer is among the early adopters of this Cloud Ready Mode. 
 The decision wasn't just about replacing software. The customer had clear requirements around data quality, compliance, and long-term maintainability. As the Head of Master Data put it the real question was never "Does it work?" but "Is it future-proof?" . That framing shaped the entire project. 
 The team was a mix of customer business stakeholders, the implementation partner, and SAP. I was involved on the SAP side as Trusted Advisor and/or Solution expert. The project ran on time and without major disruptions, which (...let's be honest..) is not always a given in this space. 
 Key Innovations Introduced 
 Beyond replacing the old system, the project introduced capabilities that deliver measurable value day-to-day: 
 The Dun & Bradstreet integration stands out. Native enrichment directly in MDG means business partner data is cleaner from the start and the creation process is faster. Not a workaround, not a custom interface! - a standard integration that works. SAP MDG enables this through the Flexible Data Provider Integration , introduced with version 2025. The required CPI mappings were handled by a dedicated CPI expert. 
 DQM derivations were another real win. Business rules automatically populate default values based on existing data, cutting down manual effort significantly. With a small enhancement on SAP BTP, the result of the derivations are visible to the requestor of the master data object as a task in his Inbox. 
 Rule-based SAP BTP workflow with a rule-based agent and flow determination to support the requirements of the customer for a flexible approval/governance process. 
 And from an architecture perspective: MDG co-deployed on the existing S/4HANA system keeps the landscape clean and reduces TCO considerably compared to a standalone setup. 
 Where Things Could Go Next 
 With Cloud Ready Mode now in place, the foundation is set for future enhancements. Possible directions include: 
 AI-powered process automation to further increase process performance and user satisfaction 
 Federated governance across a broader group structure, extending the model beyond the initial scope 
 Continuous data quality improvements building on the existing DQM and D&B foundation 
 What Was Achieved and What Was Learned 
 The project showed that master data governance is far more than a software implementation: It is also organizational development . My key findings at a glance: 
 Transparent, trustworthy business partner data as the foundation for quality and compliance 
 Improved data quality and processes: not just "get clean" , but "stay clean" 
 Reduced complexity through standardization and Clean Core (direct reduction in operating costs) 
 Native D&B enrichment is a real, measurable added value 
 Centralization does not automatically solve governance: What matters is the right mix of centralization and federation 
 "Keep it simple" - complexity is the greatest enemy of sustainable master data governance 
 MDG Cloud Ready Mode is production-ready. It's more flexible and extensible than many people think.. 
 The customer is very satisfied with the project and the SAP software — and has chosen to present it as a success story at the DSAG Annual Congress 2026 . (see https://lnkd.in/p/eBTGCC5i ) 
 best regards 
 Steffen

items.title: Beyond Configuration. Built for Decisions. | Rethinking SAP IBP vs. S/4HANA
items.author: rahulmohnot
items.text:
S/4HANA powers execution. SAP IBP helps shape the decisions behind it. A perspective on what this means for implementation leaders. 

 THOUGHT LEADERSHIP / SAP IBP 

 Beyond Configuration. 
 Built for Decisions. 
 Why SAP IBP should be approached as a decision-modeling discipline, not simply another configuration project. 

 A well-run business needs both a reliable system of execution and a sound way to decide what to execute. 
 That is the subtle but consequential difference between the implementation emphasis of SAP S/4HANA and SAP Integrated Business Planning (IBP) . 

 SAP S/4HANA 
 Design for execution 
 Structures business processes, transactions and controls for reliable day-to-day operations. 
 SAP IBP 
 Design for decisions 
 Models assumptions, constraints and trade-offs to evaluate future plans before execution. 

 A configured planning system is not necessarily a trustworthy planning model. 
 A single SAP IBP key figure can require decisions about calculation levels, aggregation logic, business assumptions and scenario behavior. The formula may be simple. Proving the answer is right across the enterprise is not. 
 My white paper explores why that distinction changes how we scope, staff, validate and govern an IBP implementation. 

 “S/4HANA helps execute business decisions. SAP IBP helps determine which decisions make business sense before they are executed.” 

 If you are leading an enterprise planning transformation, I invite you to read the attached paper: 
 Beyond Configuration. Built for Decisions. 
 The Hidden Complexity of SAP IBP: Why Enterprise Planning Is Modeled, Not Selected from a Menu 

 Rahul Mohnot 
 Senior SAP IBP Supply Chain Consultant & Solution Architect 
 A perspective on typical implementation emphasis; both SAP platforms remain complementary and require rigorous architecture.

items.title: I counted the released APIs in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. The BAPI numbers surprised me
items.author: AlexandrePassarelli
items.text: My students keep asking: can I use this in ABAP Cloud? So I counted every release state in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. Out of 5,487 BAPI function modules, 19 are released, 148 are explicitly "not to be released", and the other 5,320 have no entry at all. What that means in practice, and where SAP points you instead.

items.title: Fiori Elements OData V2: Incorrect object-page header and navigation hierarchy in a nested RAP BO
items.author: Shadab_Hussain67
items.text:
I am developing a custom transactional application using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. The application uses managed RAP business objects, CDS view entities, projection views, behavior definitions, and a Fiori Elements UI exposed through an OData V2 UI service. 
 My business object has the following composition hierarchy: 

 Customer — root entity 

 Customer Role — child of Customer 

 Customer Address — child of Customer 

 Company Code — child of Customer 

 Tax — child of Company Code 
 The entities have technical UUID keys, and the child entities are connected through RAP compositions and parent associations. 

 Issue 
 The application displays object pages, but the navigation hierarchy and object-page header are not behaving as expected. 
 For example, on the Customer Address object page, the header displays a slash-separated value resembling: 
 8001 / 
 On the Tax object page, the header displays: 
 8001 / / 
 The navigation/header behavior appears inconsistent across the composition hierarchy. I want to understand whether this is caused by the RAP composition and association definitions, CDS annotations, or the way Fiori Elements resolves object-page navigation context. 

 Questions 

 How does Fiori Elements determine the slash-separated header and navigation context for nested RAP composition entities? 

 What could cause the object-page header or navigation hierarchy to display incomplete or unexpected values? 

 Which RAP composition, parent-association, projection, or UI annotation settings should be checked to ensure navigation works correctly across multiple composition levels?

digest.headline: Thin day: a BAPI release-state count for S/4HANA 2023 and an unanswered nested RAP header question; two other posts have no usable content.
digest.overview:
Four items were collected, and only two have substance. A community blog counted release states across 5,487 BAPI function modules in an S/4HANA 2023 lab: 19 released, 148 marked 'not to be released', and 5,320 with no entry. A Q&A post asks why Fiori Elements OData V2 object pages show headers like '8001 /' and '8001 / /' in a nested managed RAP business object.

The other two items, an MCP OAuth post for Cloud Foundry and a 'Fluid API for Abapsmith' post, have only a title or a single sentence, so nothing can be concluded from them. The practical takeaways are to treat a missing release entry as 'not released for ABAP Cloud', and to debug nested RAP headers by checking `@UI.headerInfo` sources per entity. The BAPI figures are one author's lab count, and the method is not described.

deep_dives.title: Reading release states and what 'no entry' means in ABAP Cloud
deep_dives.explanation:
The BAPI count shows 19 released, 148 'not to be released' and 5,320 with no release entry among 5,487 function modules. In ABAP Cloud (language version 'ABAP for Cloud Development'), only objects with a C1 release contract for cloud use can be referenced. An object with no entry has no such contract, so it is not available.

In ADT, you can see an object's API state in the Properties view, on the API State tab. It shows the contracts, such as C0 for extensibility and C1 for system-internal use, and the release state of each. Also check whether SAP names a successor object. For a 'not to be released' object, the successor is usually a released CDS view, a RAP business object, or a released class.

The post does not say how the counts were read. A common way to read this data is through the release-state information in the system, but that is an assumption, not something the post states. Use the figures as a lab snapshot and verify in your own system.

deep_dives.title: Debugging header information in nested RAP projections
deep_dives.explanation:
The Fiori Elements object page header comes from `@UI.headerInfo` on the projection view of each entity. It has `typeName`, `typeNamePlural`, `title.value` and `description.value`. If these point to fields combined with separators, an empty child value leaves a trailing '/'. That matches '8001 /' and '8001 / /', although the post does not show the code.

Check these, entity by entity. First, which field each `title` and `description` references. Second, whether that field is populated on the child rows, or only on the root. Third, whether the parent association is exposed in the projection (`_Customer` with `redirected to parent`) and the composition is declared with `redirected to composition child` in the parent projection.

If you want parent values on a child page, add them to the child view through the parent association, for example `_Customer.CustomerNumber`. Do not rely on navigation context to supply them. This is a debugging approach, not a confirmed diagnosis for this case.

interview_questions.question: A colleague wants to call a BAPI from a class written in ABAP Cloud development. How do you decide whether that is allowed?
interview_questions.answer: ABAP Cloud only allows use of objects that have a release contract for cloud use (C1). I would open the BAPI in ADT and look at the API State in its properties. If it has no release entry, it is not released for ABAP Cloud, even though it works on-premise. The same is true if it is marked 'not to be released'. Only a small share of BAPIs are released: one lab count found 19 of 5,487. If it is not released, I would look for a released successor such as a released CDS view or RAP business object. If none exists, a wrapper in a classic-language-version class may be an option, called through a released interface. That keeps the cloud-ready code clean.

interview_questions.question: What does 'no release entry' mean for an object, and how does it differ from 'not to be released'?
interview_questions.answer: 'Not to be released' is an explicit statement that SAP does not intend to release the object, so it should not be expected to become available. 'No entry' means no release state has been assigned. For ABAP Cloud the effect is the same: you cannot use either. The difference is in planning. A not-to-be-released object will not become usable, so you should plan a replacement. A no-entry object might be released later, but you cannot rely on that. In one lab count, about 97% of BAPIs had no entry and about 2.7% were explicitly not to be released.

interview_questions.question: In a three-level managed RAP BO, child object pages show headers like '8001 / /'. How would you investigate?
interview_questions.answer: I would start with the `@UI.headerInfo` annotation on the projection view of each affected entity. I would list which fields feed `title` and `description`. Then I would check whether those fields are populated for child rows, since an empty value leaves a trailing separator. Next I would check the composition and parent association definitions in the BDEF and the projection views, including redirection to the parent and child projections. I would also look at the facet and line item annotations for the children. If the parent value is needed on the child page, I would expose it as a field through the parent association. I would want the actual code before concluding, because the post gives none.
